notes: A PoiTouch at the Flood-Bride (sedgemire.gd the_flood_bride). The weavers' bowl for a knot: tying one and asking the flood for clear water lifts the fog (the weather effect), as often as it is paid for.

look.speaker: The Bride's hem
look.text: Her hem, close to: bundles of reed as thick as your arm, bound with withy, and on every bundle cords tied by the hundred, rush and wool and gut, rags of indigo, a ribbon, a child's hair-band, a bootlace. A wooden bowl sits on a stake at her feet with marks in it. Over your head her arms go out over the black water, and the mere is so still you can hear the reed creak as she leans.

choices.text: Put five marks in the bowl, tie a knot, and ask the flood to lift its veil.
Tie a knot for somebody the water has.
Look at the cord that is wet.

veil.speaker: The Bride's hem
veil.text: You tie the knot the way the weavers showed you, round and through and back, and say what they say: lift your veil, so she can see you. For a moment nothing. Then the mere breathes out, and the fog goes off it in a long pale sheet toward the sea, and the Delta stands up out of it for a mile in every direction, every pole and roof and channel, very clear and very small.

knot.speaker: The Bride's hem
knot.text: You tie it low on the hem where the knots are thickest, for somebody the water has. Nothing happens. The reed creaks. But the next time you look at the bride you can find your knot at once among the thousands, the way you can find a face you know in a crowd.

wet.speaker: The Bride's hem
wet.text: One cord in the hem is dark with wet to the knot, though the hem hangs a yard over the water and it has not rained. The knot is in no weave the weavers use: a sailor's hitch, tied by somebody used to tying it in the dark. It smells of the sea, which is three miles off.

notes: A PoiTouch at the Wisp-Catcher's Rack (sedgemire.gd wisp_catchers_rack). Lore, and a choice to unstop the cracked jar's neighbours; Ferrit sells the jars.

look.speaker: The jars
look.text: Up close the jars are ordinary: Isseva pickling-glass, stoppered with wax and tied with rush. In each one a light the size of a plum turns slowly in salt water, cold green, and when you lean close it turns to the side of the glass you are on. They all do. Forty of them, all turned toward you, very slightly brighter.

choices.text: Unstop one and let it go.
Look at the cracked jar at the end.

free.speaker: The jars
free.text: The wax comes away with your thumbnail. For a heartbeat the light stays in the jar as if it does not know it can leave. Then it is out, and up, and over the reeds, low, the way a lantern goes when it is carried by somebody walking fast; and every jar on the rack goes dark for a breath, and comes back.

cracked.speaker: The jars
cracked.text: The end jar is cracked from the neck to the base and empty, the salt water dried to a white tide-line inside it. Its cord is knotted in the Lissa weave, the bittern's loops, the same knot as on the watch-rope at Heron Watch. Ferrit has not taken it down.

notes: A PoiTouch at the Flood-Mark (sedgemire.gd the_flood_mark). Reads the gauge.

look.speaker: The gauge
look.text: The gauge is a plank of white-painted oak bound to the needle with iron, notched every quarter-foot from the plinth up to twice a man's height and then plain to the top. The spring tides are cut on it in red, two hundred years of them, a hand's breadth of red notches packed close as a comb low on the plank. Far above them, near the needle's top, the Builders' line goes round the stone, filled white with salt.

choices.text: Look up at the Builders' line.

notches.speaker: The gauge
notches.text: Each is a spring tide, cut at the height the float stood, with the watcher's mark beside it. The oldest are at the bottom and the newest at the top, and if you lay a finger flat against the plank you can feel it: they climb. Not much. A finger's breadth from the first to the last. Two hundred years.

new.speaker: The gauge
new.text: Above the highest red notch somebody has cut another, a hand's breadth higher, deep and clean, with a knife that was not Hesk's: hers leave a little hook at the end of the stroke, and this has none. There is no watcher's mark beside it. There is a smear of black mud on the plank under it, as if whoever cut it had climbed up out of the water to do it.

line.speaker: The gauge
line.text: Thirteen metres up, by the ladder's rungs. The Builders cut it deep and level all the way round, and the spray off the channel has filled it with salt, so that from the water it shows as a thin white ring on a black needle. The reedfolk call it the Flood-Mark. If it marks a flood, the water stood once over every roof in the Delta and over the Nave's door.

notes: A PoiTouch at Hask's Ropewalk (sedgemire.gd hask_ropewalk). Walking a name into a rope: the Hasks' custom; a rope with a name in it once a game.

look.speaker: The wheel
look.text: The great wheel stands under the lean-to with its handle worn bright, and the whirl-board in front of it with three hooks, and the three strands going away down the walk on their trestles, taut, sixty paces to the sledge. If you turn the wheel the hooks spin, and the strands twist, and the sledge creeps up the walk toward you as the rope lays itself.

choices.text: Turn the wheel and say a name into the twist.
Turn the wheel for the feel of it.

name.speaker: The wheel
name.text: You turn, and the hooks sing, and down the walk the strands tighten and begin to lay round each other, and you say the name into it the way the Hasks do, once at every turn, until the sledge is at your feet. Corra Hask cuts the rope off the hooks without a word, whips its ends, ties an indigo rag on it, and puts it in your hands. 'It holds now,' she says. 'Whatever you tie with it.'

turn.speaker: The wheel
turn.text: The wheel is heavier than it looks and then, once it is going, lighter. The strands hum on their pegs all the way down the walk. A heron gets up off the far end and goes away low over the reeds, offended.

notes: A PoiTouch at the middle of the Unwinding (sedgemire.gd the_unwinding). Laying a grief down; the first cord is laid here in core:quest/the_first_cord (its choice is Edda Moye's, at the gate).

look.speaker: The grief-stone
look.text: The middle of the Unwinding: a pool no wider than a table, black and perfectly still, and beside it a flat grey stone worn into a hollow by knees. The hedges are higher than your head all round and the pole goes up out of the middle with its ribbons hanging in no wind. It is very quiet. Five times round, and the road and the reeds and everything else are a long way off.

choices.text: Kneel and say the thing you cannot say.
Lay the Name-Wife's first cord on the stone.

said.speaker: The grief-stone
said.text: You say it. It goes into the water and does not come back up. Nobody heard it. When you stand, your knees are wet and the path out is the same path you came in by, and it is shorter going out; everybody says so, and it is true.

cord.speaker: The grief-stone
cord.text: You lay it on the stone. A cord of rush, very old, knotted in no weave at all: one knot, tied by somebody who did not yet know how. Nothing happens. The pool does not move. Edda Moye is at the gate, waiting, and you know without being told that she will ask what you did with it.

pool.speaker: The grief-stone
pool.text: Black, and still, and deeper than a pool that size should be. Your face in it, and the pole over your head, and the ribbons. For a moment, behind your shoulder in the water, somebody else's face, an old woman's, looking where you are looking; and then only the ribbons.

notes: A PoiTouch at the Grey Heronry (sedgemire.gd the_grey_heronry): this morning's flight.

look.speaker: The slate
look.text: A slate on a post by the hide's door, chalked in Pell Oduin's square hand. A row of strokes for the herons that went up at dawn, an arrow for the way they went, a row for the ones that came back. This morning's: forty-one strokes, an arrow west, twenty strokes. Under it: 'all of them west, to the old water, and only half came back'. Under that, older and half rubbed out: 'the Bride turned'.

notes: A PoiTouch at the Sundew Garden (sedgemire.gd sundew_garden). Feeding the Mother Sundew an eel liver gives a phial of her dew; as often as you bring one.

look.speaker: The Mother Sundew
look.text: The Mother Sundew fills her tub: sixteen leaves as long as your arm, red, every hair on them tipped with a bead of dew that catches the light like glass. The flies over the garden do not come near her. On the tub's rim, a boot, laces still tied. Nelle Saye's tweezers hang on a nail by the tub, as long as a sword.

choices.text: Feed her an eel liver with the tweezers.

fed.speaker: The Mother Sundew
fed.text: You hold the liver out at the full length of the tweezers. The nearest leaf lifts to meet it before it is over the tub, and folds, slowly, over it and over the tweezers' tips, and you have to pull. When the leaf opens again the liver is gone and the dew on it has run down into a cup at its base, clear as gin. It goes into a phial. It smells of nothing at all.

boot.speaker: The Mother Sundew
boot.text: A good boot, Tollmere make, the kind the Guild's bailiffs wear, the laces still tied in a bow. It is quite dry. There is nothing in it. Nelle Saye says it was there in the morning, and that she does not want to talk about it.

notes: The Great Dredge's hook (site.hook, a notice post by the shaft). Tells, and points at Wenna Corley at the crew's fire.

look.speaker: The crew's tally-board
look.text: A board on a post by the shaft with a row of holes along the top for the crew's pegs and two columns under them: ABOVE and BELOW. Fourteen pegs, each with a name burnt into its head: TULL, ORMESBY, GAUNT, the two KETTLES, PRIOR. Every peg is in BELOW. Chalked across the bottom of the board, in a careful hand, every day for three weeks, the date and the words: NONE UP. W.C.

notes: The Keel-Barrow's hook (site.hook, a notice post by the mooring-stake). Tells; the quest is Hesk Vaurel's, at the Flood-Mark.

look.speaker: The mooring-rope
look.text: The mooring-rope runs from the ring-bolt in the barrow's stem-post out across the flats to this stake, and it is taut, humming a little in the wind, as if something at the other end were pulling on it. Something is: the stake leans seaward and the turf round its foot is torn. Nailed to the stake, a slate in a tide-watcher's hand: STEM TURNED 3 FINGERS SINCE THE NEW MOON. BY THE SPRING SHE POINTS OUT. DO NOT CUT THIS ROPE. H.V.

notes: The Flood-Bride. Lore; the knot in the hem is the touch's (core:dialogue/flood_bride_hem).

greet.speaker: Orrin Vasse
greet.text: Mind the frame; it's next year's. — You've come to look at her. Everybody comes to look at her this spring. Forty brides I've walked out, and this is the first that's been looked at.

choices.text: Who are the people in the water at night?
What does the knot in the hem do?
I'll leave you to your weaving.

why.speaker: Orrin Vasse
why.text: Because the Tide's a shore and the sea went out, and what goes out comes back, says the Tide. You don't stop the sea. You court it. — A bride a year, so it has something here it wants, and keeps to its own side waiting for her. It's worked for four hundred years, if you count it that way. I don't. I weave them anyway.

turned.speaker: Orrin Vasse
turned.text: In the night, the third week after the walking-out. We stand her facing the water, always, her arms out to it. In the morning she was facing the land, every bundle of her, and her feet in the same holes. Nobody turned her; four men couldn't. — The hem was wet to the knee. — I've told the Council. The Council said, Orrin, the Council is not a weather.

guests.speaker: Orrin Vasse
guests.text: The drowned. They come up at dark and stand in front of her in rows, quiet, as if they were waiting for somebody to come down the aisle. They don't come for me. They don't come for the house. Stand between them and her and they will, though; the eel-boy found that out, and he's lucky he's an eel-boy and can swim.

knot.speaker: Orrin Vasse
knot.text: A knot in her hem is a word to the flood. Tie one for somebody the water has and they're at the wedding; that's all; it's a kindness. — And there's the other, that the weavers don't tell the Council about: five marks in the bowl and a knot, and ask the flood to lift its veil, and it does. The fog goes off the mere like a sheet off a bed. For an hour or so. Don't ask me how. I only weave her.

greetings.text: Thirty-nine. There were forty. I counted twice. — I know it was you. They all looked at you when you came up the path.

greet.speaker: Ferrit Oache
greet.text: Don't tap the glass. — Ferrit Oache. If you want a light that never wants oil, I've the only ones in the Delta. If you want to tell me it's wicked, the Council's been, and the Callers have been, and the lantern-wrights' guild has been twice, and I'm still here.

choices.text: The wild ones come to the rack at night?

what.speaker: Ferrit Oache
what.text: Lights. — The reedfolk'll tell you they're what goes out of a drowned man when his lantern does, and they'd know, I suppose, they've drowned more men than I have. I've never caught one that spoke. I've caught one that hummed. — They don't want oil and they don't want feeding. They want salt water and the dark. They go dim if you talk about them. Like that. See.

how.speaker: Ferrit Oache
how.text: Dark of the moon, out on the North Fen, a net of eel-skin, a jar of salt water. You stand still in the reeds with your lantern out. They come to see who's there; they always come to see who's there. Then you're quick, or you're in the water, and if you're in the water they hold your head under to have a look at you. — I'm quick.

wild.speaker: Ferrit Oache
wild.text: Since the spring. Two or three, then a dozen, drifting round the rack after midnight, low. And the jarred ones go dim while they're here and bright when they've gone. I'm not a fool; I know what it looks like. It looks like visiting. — Kill one if you like; they're not mine. The glim off it's worth something to me.

cracked.speaker: Ferrit Oache
cracked.text: Number forty. A big one I took off the Gullhithe flats last autumn, where the Moreva boats go over. It cracked its jar the first night of the spring tide and went. — The cord's the Lissa weave because Tuo Lissa at the watch sold me the cord. That's all. That's all it is.

bye.speaker: Ferrit Oache
bye.text: Don't tap the glass on your way past.

notes: The Flood-Mark. Gives core:quest/the_keel_barrow; takes the Builders' plate in core:quest/the_line_on_the_needle (the plate is handed over by the next conversation, QuestRoutes) and decides both.

greetings.text: The stem's not moved a hair since you drove the pin. I measure it every morning anyway. You don't stop measuring a thing because it's stopped.
The stake was gone in the morning, and the rope, and the stem points straight out to sea and not a finger further. She's facing home. I think that's all she wanted.
There it is, up on the gauge where the Builders put it, in my hand now. The children come and look at it. It's done them no harm. It's done me some good.

greet.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
greet.text: If you've come to tell me the tide's out, I know. — Hesk Vaurel. Tide-Watcher. The last one. Sit down if you want; the bench is wet, it's always wet.

choices.text: You put a slate on a stake by the Keel-Barrow.
I've put the Keel-King down. I have his steering-pin.
I have a Builders' plate from the Great Dredge's shaft.
I'll leave you to the water.

gauge.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
gauge.text: The spring tides. Every one for two hundred years, at the height the float stood, notched with the watcher's mark. Mine are the top forty. — They climb. A finger's breadth since the first. That's nothing. That's a wet summer. — Except they never once go down.

new_notch.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
new_notch.text: Not me. I'd know my own stroke; I've a hook at the end of it like my mother had. That one's clean. Cut at the top of the spring tide three nights back, in the dark, by somebody who came up out of the channel to do it and went back into it. — There's mud on the plank. There are no footprints on the bank.

q_offer.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_offer.text: The Keel-Barrow, on the flats past the Saltgate. The Salt Isles' king in his ship under the turf. — Her stem's turning. I've measured it every morning since the new moon: three fingers, toward the sea, a finger a night at the springs. By the next spring tide she'll point straight out. — Somebody's tied a mooring-rope to her stem and it pulls. And the drowned come up the flats at dark and stand at her side like a crew waiting to be piped aboard. — I don't want to see what sails. Go into her. Whatever is turning her, it's in the hold.

q_accept.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_accept.text: There's a door in her side, boards gone white with the salt, on the landward side. The Salt Isles put a crew in with him, at the oars. Mind the hold; it's under water at the springs and the sallowjaws have found it. — He'll be at the steering-oar. Kings always are.

q_barrow_decide.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_barrow_decide.text: — Iron. Salt Isles iron, black, wet; it's cold. That's the pin out of the steering-oar's head, that holds the oar to the ship. — With it out of his hand she can't steer, so the stem's stopped. You can feel it, can't you, down on the flats. Nothing pulling. — It goes one of three ways. Drive it back into her stem-post and she's moored where she lies, for good. Cut the rope and give the pin to the sea at the ebb, and she points home and the drowned can go aboard and nobody's sorry. Or keep it, and she's neither, and that's your business.

choices.text: Drive it back into the stem. She stays moored.
Cut the rope. Give the pin to the sea.

q_barrow_pinned.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_barrow_pinned.text: Moored. Yes. The Delta's been her harbour four hundred years; it can be another four. I'll come with you and hold the lantern. — I'll put her on the gauge: a notch for the day she stopped.

q_barrow_cut.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_barrow_cut.text: Home, then. — It's what I'd want. I'd want to face home. — Cut it at the stake, not the ring; she'll take the rope with her. Throw the pin out past the Tideflat Stones at the bottom of the ebb, and don't watch where it goes in.

q_barrow_kept.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_barrow_kept.text: — Your business. I said so. — Don't sleep with it under your pillow. Don't sleep near water with it at all, if you can help it.

q_needle_offer.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_offer.text: Show me. — Give it here. — It's the line. It's the needle's line, cut in a plate of the same stone, with the Builders' marks on either side of it that nobody can read and I can read some of. — Leave it with me. Come back. I'll need a night with it, and a candle, and to not be talked to.

q_needle_accept.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_accept.text: Give it to me when you're ready, and then go away for a night.

q_needle_decide.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_decide.text: I've read it. Some of it. — The line is the flood. It's the height the water stood once, over every roof in the Delta and the Nave's door. And these marks either side of it are a count, the same count as the notches, tides; and the count's not finished. — It says when, near enough. Not soon. Not never. — I don't know what to do with it. You brought it up out of the ground. You say.

choices.text: Cut the line into the gauge, so the watchers know what they're watching for.
Drop the plate down the float-well. Let the water keep it.
Take it to the Reed Council in Isseva. It's theirs to tell.

q_needle_cut.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_cut.text: On the gauge. Where anybody can read it. — Yes. A watcher who doesn't know what she's watching for is only a woman sitting on a wet bench. I'll cut it tomorrow at the ebb, and put my mark beside it.

q_needle_sunk.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_sunk.text: Down the well. — It'll be safe there. The float will sit on it every tide. That's a kind of watching too.

q_needle_council.speaker: Hesk Vaurel
q_needle_council.text: The Council. Hm. They'll call a meeting about it and the meeting will last a year. — That's all right. A year's nothing, to the plate.

notes: Hask's Ropewalk; sells rope (core:table/stock_ropewalk). Takes Iven Hask's token in core:quest/iven_hasks_rope (handed over by the next conversation) and decides it.

greetings.text: I walk his name in every morning now, first rope of the day. It holds better. They all hold better. Don't tell my customers it's because I'm crying into the twist.

greet.speaker: Corra Hask
greet.text: Three hundred and eleven, three hundred and twelve— sorry. Paces. — Corra Hask. If it's rope, it's here. If it's a name, it's here too: say it at the wheel and I'll walk it in.

choices.text: Why walk a name into a rope?
Whose is the rope with the grey rag?
I found this in the Keel-Barrow. It has your name on it.

names.speaker: Corra Hask
names.text: Because a rope's only a promise, and a promise wants somebody's name on it. — My grandmother said a boat tied with a named rope never drifts, and a lantern hung on one never goes out before its verse. I don't know. Nobody's ever come back to complain.

iven.speaker: Corra Hask
iven.text: My brother's. Iven. — He went down to the Outfall nine years ago to ship with a Salt Isles boat that came in out of season, all black sails. Wanted to see the Isles. She sailed on the ebb and he wasn't on her when the Saeva men looked, and he wasn't anywhere after. — I walked his name into that rope the day he went, for luck. It's for him when he comes home. It's been a long time coming home.

q_offer.speaker: Corra Hask
q_offer.text: — That's a Hask token. That's ours. We stamp one for every walker, so the buyer knows who walked it. That's Iven's; that's his notch on the back, he cut it crooked the day he was given it. — In the barrow. With the king's crew. At the oars. — Give it here. Give it here, I want to hold it.

q_accept.speaker: Corra Hask
q_accept.text: Put it in my hand. — Then sit down a minute. Don't say anything.

q_decide.speaker: Corra Hask
q_decide.text: So he's there. On the bench with the old king's crew, rowing nowhere. — His rope's on the rack. It has his name in it. — I could walk it out to the barrow and lay it on the stem where they muster, so he has his own rope at last. Or I could cut it up and walk him into every rope I make from now, so his name goes out in every boat in Isseva. — You found him. You say which.

choices.text: Lay his rope at the Keel-Barrow. I'll carry it.
Walk his name into every rope you make.

q_decide_carry.speaker: Corra Hask
q_decide_carry.text: Take it, then. Lay it on the stem where they stand at night. Tie it to nothing. — He'll know it. It's his name.

q_decide_walk.speaker: Corra Hask
q_decide_walk.text: Every rope. Every boat in Isseva tied up with Iven Hask. — He wanted to see the world. That's the most of it he'll get. It's a lot of boats.

notes: The Unwinding. Decides core:quest/the_first_cord with whoever walked the Name-Wife's first cord in.

greetings.text: I raked the path after you. There was one set of footprints going out, as there should be. And one more, small, bare, that I've never seen before, going out ahead of yours.

greet.speaker: Edda Moye
greet.text: In is to the left of the gate; it always is. — Edda Moye. I keep the hedges. If you've come to walk it, walk it; I'll not ask what you're carrying.

choices.text: Why have you never walked it?
Whose is the cord on the pole?
I laid the Name-Wife's first cord at the pool.
I'll leave you to your rake.

middle.speaker: Edda Moye
middle.text: A pool and a stone. You kneel on the stone and you say it to the pool, the thing you can't say, and the water has it and you don't. Then you walk out. That's all. — People come out lighter. Some come out the same and walk it again. One came out and asked me where he was, and I told him, and he cried, and went home.

never.speaker: Edda Moye
never.text: My man and both my boys are in the water off Gullhithe. Thirty years. — If I walk it I'll put them down. I'm not ready to put them down. I'm saving it. — I'll know when. I'll know because I'll want to.

cord.speaker: Edda Moye
cord.text: Somebody tied it on the pole in the spring and didn't come out the gate. I raked the path; one set of prints going in and none coming out. — It's knotted the way the Name-Wife knots hers, in a family's weave. Somebody brought a name here to put it down and couldn't, and left it on the pole instead.

q_decide.speaker: Edda Moye
q_decide.text: On the stone. — Let me see it. — That's no weave at all. That's one knot, tied by somebody learning. A child's knot. — That's her own name. The first she ever took, and it was her own, to see if it could be done. — It's on the stone at the middle now. What do you want done with it? It's yours to say; you carried it in.

choices.text: Say it into the pool, whatever it was, and let the water have it.
Tie it on the pole with the ribbons. Unsaid, but kept.

q_decide_walked.speaker: Edda Moye
q_decide_walked.text: Then it's said, and it's gone, and she's nobody's and nothing's and at rest. — I'll rake after you. Go on out. It's shorter going out.

q_decide_hung.speaker: Edda Moye
q_decide_hung.text: On the pole. With the others nobody could say. — She'll be in good company. The ribbons are all for the ones that couldn't be let go of.

q_decide_kept.speaker: Edda Moye
q_decide_kept.text: Keep it. — Careful who you show it to. A name's a heavy thing in a pocket, and that one's heavier than most.

notes: The Grey Heronry. Reads a flight for five marks, and each reading finds the next of Sedgemire's new places on the chart (discover), in order.

greet.speaker: Pell Oduin
greet.text: Shh. — No, it's all right, they've gone up. Pell Oduin. I read the herons. Sit, if you've come to be read for; stand, if you've come to laugh, and do it quietly.

know.speaker: Pell Oduin
know.text: Where something new has come into the fen. They go to look at it; they're curious birds and they're not frightened of much. A new boat, a new grave, a dead sallowjaw, a door that's opened. — The Council pays me to say where they went. It's not magic. It's herons.

half.speaker: Pell Oduin
half.text: This morning. All of them west at the dawn, to the old water past the Saltgate where the Salt Isles' barrow is, and twenty back. Twenty-one didn't come home. — Herons don't drown. I've watched them thirty years. They don't drown.

read_0.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_0.text: Sit. — There. Watch them go up. ... Forty, forty-one. And off, west, low, the whole flight over the flats past the Saltgate to the long barrow with the ship's posts, and round it three times. — They go to look at what's new. Something there is new, or newly old. That's where you'll find it, if you go. That's all a heron-reader is for.

read_1.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_1.text: Sit. — There. Watch them go up. ... Forty, forty-one. And off, west of Isseva, where the Guild's crane stands over the shaft; they went round it and would not settle. — They go to look at what's new. Something there is new, or newly old. That's where you'll find it, if you go. That's all a heron-reader is for.

read_2.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_2.text: Sit. — There. Watch them go up. ... Forty, forty-one. And off, down the channel to the Builders' needle at Oulea, and stood along its plinth in a row, facing the sea. — They go to look at what's new. Something there is new, or newly old. That's where you'll find it, if you go. That's all a heron-reader is for.

read_3.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_3.text: Sit. — There. Watch them go up. ... Forty, forty-one. And off, south, over Nauvissa, to the round of reed hedges, and one came down at the middle and stood there an hour. — They go to look at what's new. Something there is new, or newly old. That's where you'll find it, if you go. That's all a heron-reader is for.

read_4.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_4.text: Sit. — There. Watch them go up. ... Forty, forty-one. And off, east over the Lantern Causeway to Hask's island, and sat along the ropewalk's trestles like knots. — They go to look at what's new. Something there is new, or newly old. That's where you'll find it, if you go. That's all a heron-reader is for.

read_done.speaker: Pell Oduin
read_done.text: Sit. — Up they go. ... And round, and back to the alders, every one. — Nothing new in the fen today that you haven't seen. That's a good flight. I'll not take marks for a good flight.

notes: The Sundew Garden; sells dew and sundew (core:table/stock_sundew_garden). Feeding the Mother is the touch's (core:dialogue/mother_sundew).

greet.speaker: Nelle Saye
greet.text: Don't touch the beds, and don't touch the Mother, and don't touch the jars without paying. — Nelle Saye. You'll be wanting dew. Everybody wants dew.

dew.speaker: Nelle Saye
dew.text: Glue, for the lantern-wrights; the horn panes go in with it and never come out. Salve, for the bleeders; it shuts a leech-bite in a breath. And a drop in water is a sleep with no dreams in it, which the widows buy. — The Mother's dew is better than all of it. Feed her an eel liver and I'll bottle what comes off her. No charge. She's earned it more than me.

mother.speaker: Nelle Saye
mother.text: My grandmother's. She brought it as a seedling from the old garden at Mor'oul before the flood had that. It's been fed an eel a week for sixty years and grown a hand every year. — Lately it closes on the eel before the eel's dropped. I've stopped using my fingers.

boot.speaker: Nelle Saye
boot.text: I don't want to talk about the boot. — It was there in the morning. There's nobody missing. I asked. — It's a Guild boot. I've told the Guild. The Guild said, Mistress Saye, the Guild is not missing a bailiff. — I've not fed her since. She doesn't seem to mind.

bye.speaker: Nelle Saye
bye.text: Mind your hands near the tub.

notes: The Great Dredge. Gives core:quest/the_great_dredge and decides it; starts core:quest/the_line_on_the_needle when the plate is to go to Hesk Vaurel.

greetings.text: The chain went down the shaft like a snake going home. I took the pegs off the board and put them in the pot and boiled them, which is a Tollmere thing and I'll not explain it. — I'm going home on the next barge.
The new crew comes up the channel on the next spring tide. Twelve men. I'll keep their board. I'll not keep their pot.

greet.speaker: Wenna Corley
greet.text: You're not Guild. — Good. Sit by the fire; there's stew, there's always stew, there's stew for fourteen. Wenna Corley. I keep the board.

choices.text: I've been down. Brannoc Tull is dead. I have his tally.

down.speaker: Wenna Corley
down.text: The Builders' street. Eight metres down under the peat, black stone, dead straight, doors off it both sides and a hall at the end with the roof still on. The engineers came up white. Brannoc said it was the best find in fifty years and the Guild would put his name on a sluice. — The peat's held the water off it all this time. Till we dug.

chain.speaker: Wenna Corley
chain.text: At night. Link by link, a click, a long wait, a click, as if somebody were coming up it hand over hand and resting. — I've sat by the shaft with the lantern. Nothing comes up. In the morning the buckets are all a link higher than they were. — I've stopped sitting by the shaft.

q_offer.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_offer.text: Change of shift. Three weeks ago tomorrow. Brannoc took the day men down to the hall to bring up the night men, all fourteen pegs in BELOW at once, which the Guild doesn't allow, and Brannoc did it anyway because it was faster. — Nobody came up. Not the day men, not the night men. Not a shout. The lantern on the ladder went out at midnight and I haven't been brave enough to light it again. — I've written to the Guild twice. The Guild says wait. — Will you go down? Bring up Brannoc's tally, at least. It's on his belt. Then the board can be closed and they can be paid.

q_accept.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_accept.text: The ladder's at the landward side of the shaft. Down to the cut, then the Guild's camp where the night men slept, then the street. Brannoc will be at the bottom; he always was. — Take the lantern off the head-frame. Light it. I couldn't.

q_decide.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_decide.text: — That's his. That's Brannoc's tally, every man notched on it. — And what's this, wired to it? Black stone. A plate, with a line cut across it and marks either side. He found it in the hall, then. He'll have wanted it shown to somebody. — There's a woman at Oulea, the Tide-Watcher, Hesk Vaurel; she reads Builders' marks, they say. — Now. The Dredge. The Guild will want it digging again by the spring, new crew, new pegs. Or the pin comes out of the sheer-legs' head and the chain goes down the shaft for good, and nobody digs there again in my lifetime. — I'm Guild. I can't say it. You say it.

choices.text: Knock the pin out. Let the chain go down the shaft for good.
Give the tally to the Guild. Let them send a new crew.
I'm keeping the tally, and saying nothing.

q_decide_break.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_decide_break.text: — Yes. — I'll hold the lantern. You knock. — Take the plate to Hesk Vaurel at Oulea. Somebody should know what Brannoc died for.

q_decide_guild.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_decide_guild.text: The Guild, then. I'll write it. They'll pay you; they pay well for what's already theirs. — Take the plate to Hesk Vaurel at Oulea before they ask for it. The Guild doesn't need to know about the plate.

q_decide_keep.speaker: Wenna Corley
q_decide_keep.text: — Keep it. Then the board stays open. Fourteen pegs in BELOW, and nobody paid. — I'll keep the pot on.

bye.speaker: Wenna Corley
bye.text: There's stew if you come back. There's always stew.
